items.prompt: What is a bird's beak made of?

options.label: Bone sheathed in keratin
options.feedback: A light bony core under a hard growing cover.

options.label: Solid bone alone
options.feedback: Bare bone would chip and never repair itself.

options.label: Hardened cartilage
options.feedback: Cartilage bends. A beak that bent would be useless.

options.label: Fused teeth and gum
options.feedback: No living bird has teeth to fuse.

items.ok_line: Bone for shape, keratin for the working edge.
items.ko_line: It has two layers: one gives the shape, the other takes the wear.
items.exp_title: A tool with a replaceable edge
items.exp_text: The beak is a projection of the skull, made of light bone honeycombed with air, covered by a sheath of keratin — the same protein as feathers and your nails. That sheath grows continuously and wears away at the tip, so the beak sharpens itself with use. A caged bird with nothing hard to work on ends up with an overgrown beak, for the same reason a rabbit's teeth overgrow without gnawing.

items.prompt: What do birds use instead of teeth to grind their food?

options.label: A muscular gizzard
options.feedback: A grinding chamber, often loaded with swallowed grit.

options.label: A very strong stomach acid
options.feedback: Acid dissolves; it cannot crack a seed husk.

options.label: Ridges along the beak
options.feedback: Some beaks have them, but the grinding is deeper in.

options.label: The muscles of the throat
options.feedback: The throat only moves food along.

items.ok_line: The grinding happens well past the beak, in a muscular mill.
items.ko_line: Birds swallow small stones on purpose. Ask yourself where those go.
items.exp_title: A mill instead of a jaw
items.exp_text: Teeth and the heavy jaw that carries them are dead weight in the air, so birds moved the work backwards. The gizzard is a thick-walled muscular chamber that crushes food, and seed-eaters swallow grit and small stones to line it, turning it into a grinding mill. Some fossil dinosaurs are found with the same worn stones in the same place. An ostrich's gizzard will reduce a swallowed pebble to sand.

items.prompt: What is a crossbill's crossed beak for?

options.label: Prising open conifer cones
options.feedback: The tips lever the scales apart, then the tongue takes the seed.

options.label: Gripping struggling prey
options.feedback: Crossed tips grip worse than straight ones.

options.label: Cutting through tough bark
options.feedback: Cutting wants a straight chisel, like a woodpecker's.

options.label: Carrying nest material
options.feedback: Any beak carries twigs. None needs crossing for it.

items.ok_line: It is a crowbar, and the cone is what it opens.
items.ko_line: Think of the crossed tips as a lever rather than as a grip.
items.exp_title: A crowbar shaped like a beak
items.exp_text: The crossbill slides its crossed tips between the scales of a closed conifer cone and twists, forcing the scales apart, then lifts the seed out with its tongue. No other small bird can open a green cone, so the crossbill feeds on a supply nobody competes for. The cross runs left in some individuals and right in others, and each bird works cones from the side that suits its own beak.

options.label: It filters water with its head upside down
options.feedback: Rows of plates strain out algae and tiny shrimp.

options.label: It spears fish in the shallows
options.feedback: That is a heron's method, with a very different beak.

options.label: It digs in mud for worms
options.feedback: Its beak is a sieve, not a probe.

options.label: It plucks seeds from the water's surface
options.feedback: The bend in the beak makes surface picking impossible.

items.ok_line: It is a sieve, and that is why the beak is bent.
items.ko_line: The odd bend in the beak only makes sense in one position.
items.exp_text: The flamingo lowers its head so the beak is inverted, then pumps water through with its tongue. Rows of hair-like plates called lamellae strain out algae and brine shrimp — the same principle a whale uses with baleen, arrived at separately. The sharp bend in the beak is what lets the two halves meet properly when the head is upside down; held the normal way up, the shape makes no sense at all.

items.prompt: Why does hammering wood not injure a woodpecker?

options.label: Its skull is built to absorb the blow
options.feedback: Spongy bone and a tongue that wraps the skull spread the shock.

options.label: It strikes far more gently than it looks
options.feedback: The impact can reach a thousand times gravity.

options.label: It closes its eyes at each strike
options.feedback: It does, but that protects the eyes, not the brain.

options.label: Its brain floats in extra fluid
options.feedback: The opposite: the brain is packed tight so it cannot rattle.

items.ok_line: The whole head is built as a shock absorber.
items.ko_line: The blow really is that hard. So the answer must be in the head itself.
items.exp_title: A head designed around the blow
items.exp_text: A woodpecker strikes up to twenty times a second at forces that would concuss a person. Its brain is small, smooth and packed tightly so it cannot slam about; the skull carries plates of spongy bone that deform slightly at impact; the two halves of the beak are unequal in length so the shock is thrown off centre. Its tongue is so long it wraps right around the back of the skull, adding one more strap of padding.

items.prompt: What is a pelican's throat pouch for?

options.label: Scooping fish along with water
options.feedback: It drains the water off, then swallows what is left.

options.label: Storing fish for the journey home
options.feedback: The catch goes down the throat, not into store.

options.label: Carrying water to the chicks
options.feedback: Chicks take fish from the parent's gullet, not water.

options.label: Making its call louder
options.feedback: Pelicans are near silent as adults.

items.ok_line: It is a net, and the water drains straight back out.
items.ko_line: It is used at the moment of the catch, not afterwards.
items.exp_text: The pouch stretches to hold far more than the stomach — up to about thirteen litres in a large pelican. The bird plunges, opens the beak, and the pouch balloons around fish and water together. It then presses the water out over the beak's edge before swallowing. The pouch doubles as a radiator: on hot days the bird flutters it to lose heat, the way a dog pants.

items.prompt: Which beak shape belongs to a seed eater?

options.label: Short, thick and conical
options.feedback: Built to crack a husk between two strong jaws.

options.label: Long, thin and curved
options.feedback: That reaches into flowers or probes deep mud.

options.label: Broad, flat and blunt
options.feedback: That sieves water, like a duck's.

options.label: Hooked and sharp-edged
options.feedback: That tears flesh. It belongs to a hunter.

items.ok_line: Short and thick means leverage, and leverage cracks a shell.
items.ko_line: Cracking a husk needs force close to the hinge, not reach.
items.exp_text: Force falls away with distance from the hinge, so a short deep beak bites far harder than a long slender one. A hawfinch cracks a cherry stone at a pressure of some fifty kilos, enough to hurt a careless finger. The rule runs right through the group: reach and precision at one end, crushing power at the other, and no beak has ever managed both.

items.prompt: What is a toucan's enormous beak mainly good for?

options.label: Reaching fruit and losing heat
options.feedback: It stretches to far twigs, and it radiates warmth.

options.label: Fighting off rival birds
options.feedback: It is too light to be a weapon; it would break.

options.label: Digging nest holes in trees
options.feedback: Toucans take over holes that woodpeckers cut.

options.label: Cracking hard nuts
options.feedback: It is hollow and light. A nut would crush it.

items.ok_line: It reaches the fruit, and it dumps heat while doing it.
items.ko_line: It is far lighter than it looks, so rule out anything needing force.
items.exp_text: The beak is a foam of bone struts under a thin keratin shell, so despite its size it weighs almost nothing. It lets a heavy bird sit on a solid branch and still reach fruit at the thin end of a twig. Thermal cameras revealed a second use: it is threaded with blood vessels the bird can open and close, dumping heat on a hot afternoon and shutting down at night. Proportionally it is the largest beak of any bird.

items.prompt: How does a hummingbird get nectar out of a flower?

options.label: Its tongue traps the nectar and pulls it in
options.feedback: The forked tip springs open and closes around the liquid.

options.label: It sucks through the beak like a straw
options.feedback: The beak is a sheath. The tongue does the work.

options.label: It bites the flower open and drinks
options.feedback: Some birds do rob flowers that way. Hummingbirds do not.

options.label: It shakes the flower and catches the drops
options.feedback: Nectar clings inside; shaking releases nothing.

items.ok_line: The beak is only the sheath. The tongue is the instrument.
items.ko_line: Watch where the beak stops and something thinner keeps going.
items.exp_title: A tongue that snaps shut on the nectar
items.exp_text: High-speed film settled a long argument. The tongue is not a straw: its forked tip springs open as it enters the nectar and snaps shut as it withdraws, trapping the liquid between two curled edges. The bird can do this some fifteen times a second. Its beak simply carries the tongue past the petals, which is why beak length matches the flowers a species feeds on so closely.

items.prompt: Why does a heron stand still for so long in shallow water?

options.label: It is waiting for a fish to come close
options.feedback: Then the neck straightens in a fraction of a second.

options.label: It is warming itself in the sun
options.feedback: Standing in cold water is a poor way to warm up.

options.label: It is stirring the mud with its feet
options.feedback: Some birds do that. A stalking heron does not move.

options.label: It is drinking slowly through its beak
options.feedback: A heron drinks in seconds, then moves on.

items.ok_line: The stillness is the hunt. The strike is the easy part.
items.ko_line: Ask what a fish would do if the bird moved at all.
items.exp_text: A heron hunts by not existing as far as the fish is concerned, sometimes for many minutes. Its neck is folded into an S held under tension by a specially shaped vertebra, so the strike takes a fraction of a second — far quicker than a fish can turn. The dagger beak grabs rather than spears in most species. It also corrects for the way water bends light, aiming at where the fish is instead of where it appears.
